title: How much is it?
goal: Ask about and understand prices, read big numbers, and see why Polish money has three forms: *złoty*, *złote*, and *złotych*.
bekal: ask prices with *ile kosztuje* and *ile płacę*
read prices in *złoty* and *grosz* with the right form

dialogs.title: Dialogue — W kiosku z biletami
dialogs.intro: The public transport ticket counter at the station. Budi wants to buy a monthly pass.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawca:
lines.text: Dzień dobry, w czym mogę pomóc?
lines.id: Good afternoon, how can I help?
lines.literal: day good, in what I-can help?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How much is a monthly ticket?

lines.speaker: Sprzedawca:
lines.text: Sto dziesięć złotych. A studencki pięćdziesiąt pięć.
lines.id: A hundred and ten złoty. The student one is fifty-five.
lines.literal: hundred ten złotys. and student's fifty five.

lines.speaker: Sprzedawca:
lines.id: Great. That'll be fifty-five złoty, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeszcze jedno pytanie. Ile kosztuje bilet jednorazowy?
lines.id: One more question. How much is a single ticket?
lines.literal: still one question. how-much costs ticket single-use?

lines.speaker: Sprzedawca:
lines.text: Trzy złote sześćdziesiąt. Proszę, to pana bilet.
lines.id: Three sixty. Here's your ticket, sir.
lines.literal: three złotys sixty. please, this sir's ticket.

notes: **Ile kosztuje** for one item, **ile kosztują** for several: *Ile kosztuje bilet?* but *Ile kosztują bilety?*. The safest form if you're unsure: *Ile to kosztuje?* — "how much is this", pointing at the item.

**Złoty, złote, złotych.** Polish currency follows the number rule you saw in Unit 6: *jeden złoty*, *dwa/trzy/cztery złote*, *pięć złotych*. The rule is exactly the same as *rok / lata / lat*, so you already have the pattern.

**Grosz** is the hundredth part, and it follows the same pattern: *jeden grosz*, *dwa grosze*, *pięć groszy*. In conversation, Poles often drop *grosze* altogether: *trzy złote sześćdziesiąt* — just like saying "three sixty" in English.

**Bilet miesięczny, bilet jednorazowy** — an adjective stands **after** the noun when it names a type, not a quality. Compare *duży bilet* (a big ticket) with *bilet miesięczny* (monthly ticket, a fixed term). The same pattern appears in *woda gazowana* and *kawa czarna* in Unit 8.
**Legitymacja studencka** — student ID. It's valuable in Poland: many discounts on transport, museums, and cinemas require it, and the discount is often half price.
**W czym mogę pomóc** literally "in what can I help". The standard line of shop staff; just answer with *poproszę…* or *szukam…*.
**Dziękuję za pomoc** — after *za* comes the object form (*pomoc* happens not to change). Ready-made pattern: *dziękuję za kawę*, *dziękuję za informację*.
**To pana bilet** — "this is your ticket, sir". The possessive for someone addressed politely isn't *twój* but *pana* (m) or *pani* (f). One of the politeness markers beginners forget most easily.

grammars.title: Money: złoty, złote, złotych
body: Three forms, chosen by the **last digit**, exactly like years in Unit 6.
after: The same rule applies to almost every counted noun: *bilet / bilety / biletów*, *książka / książki / książek*, *osoba / osoby / osób*.
An honest shortcut: if you're unsure, **just say the number without the currency**. *Ile? — Pięćdziesiąt pięć.* Poles do it all day long, and nobody will suspect you're dodging the grammar.
⚠️ The official abbreviation is **zł**, written after the number: *55 zł*. The bank code is PLN.

grammars.title: Big numbers
body: Hundreds and thousands are simply strung together in order, with no "and" in between.
after: 500–900 all end in *-set* and are written as one word. 200–400 don't, and their forms have to be learned as they are.
Combined examples: *tysiąc dwieście pięćdziesiąt* (1,250), *dwa tysiące dwadzieścia sześć* (2026).
Notice that *tysiąc* itself follows the 2-3-4 rule: *dwa tysiące*, but *pięć tysięcy*.

Meaning
rows: Do you have small change, sir?

blocks.title: Haggling in Poland?
items: In shops, supermarkets, and kiosks — **no**. Prices are fixed, and haggling would feel odd to the seller.
At flea markets (*pchli targ*) and open-air markets, haggling is normal. The phrase: *Czy może być taniej?* (can it be cheaper?).
What newcomers often forget: there are many official discounts (students, weekends, apps) that you only have to ask for — *Czy jest jakaś zniżka?*

blocks.text: Numbers aren't only for prices. These four uses come up every day in Poland.
Polish phone numbers have nine digits and are read in groups of three. The emergency number is **112**, as everywhere in the European Union.

blocks.title: Asking for a number
items: *Jaki masz numer telefonu?* — What's your phone number?
*Możesz powtórzyć wolniej?* — Can you repeat that more slowly?
*Napiszesz mi to?* — Could you write it down for me?
That last one is the most honest weapon a beginner has: numbers spoken fast are hard to catch even after a year of study.
